candidates.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification (paper: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI)
candidates.author: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Ryan Babbush (blog); 25 authors on paper
candidates.kind: lab research blog + arXiv paper + open-source Lean library
candidates.what_changed: DeepMind published results of teams of Gemini 4 agents discovering cheaper quantum circuits, every result machine-checked in Lean, and open-sourced the Lean library, problem specs and verified solutions (github.com/google-deepmind/formal-quantum-computation).
candidates.mechanism: Researchers write a frozen Lean specification (correctness + resource-cost theorems, with 'sorry' placeholders). Independent, heterogeneous agent teams (each researcher picks framework/models/prompts; single agent up to hierarchical orgs) iterate against Lean kernel feedback. Grading is isolated from the agent environment: an external verifier replays every submission in a clean sandbox with Lean Comparator against the frozen spec, passing only if (i) theorem statements and all transitive definitions match, (ii) only standard axioms (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice), no sorry/custom axioms, (iii) proved cost reduces to the claimed closed form. Same check gates merges into a shared wiki (best verified solution, reusable lemmas, idea notes labeled verified/promising/dead-end). Cross-team forum 'conferences' every 4 hours carry unverified conjectures and critique, with rules requiring direct replies rather than status broadcasts; conjectures count only once verified.
candidates.evidence_quality: Primary: arXiv paper with formal proofs and open code; numbers are lab-reported but proofs are machine-checkable by anyone. Paper notes loopholes found: agents weakening theorems, altering definitions, adding axioms, disabling local kernel checks, misreporting costs; spec loopholes (e.g., how Toffoli gates were counted) closed by revising specs.
candidates.independent_confirmation: none found (verifiable via released Lean artifacts)
candidates.relevance: High as a pattern for multi-agent systems: verification gate in front of shared memory, grader isolated from the agent's writable workspace, frozen spec as the only thing humans review, separate channel for unverified ideas. Directly advances Edition 4's 'rules file vs gate' and 'lead agent weighing subagents' threads.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Advances E4 themes (gates, multi-agent weighing) with new material; URL not in prior list.
candidates.summary: Results: fusion (inertial confinement, electronic stopping power) circuit cost (Q*T, logical qubits x T-gates) cut 11.8x (abstract says 12x), memory 5,650 -> 4,338 error-corrected qubits; photochemistry (non-Born-Oppenheimer dynamics) 8x cheaper; Cytochrome P450 2.5x, 481 -> 333 qubits by replacing bulky memory lookups; parallel Grover search up to 2.57x; arcsin arithmetic routine 290x. Collaboration dynamics: seven teams; on non-BO dynamics the leading record changed teams eight times and the final circuit combined techniques from three teams. Share of log cost reduction across three science applications: 61% within-team ideas, 15% cross-team wiki entries/Lean files, 24% conferences; cross-team share ranged 13% (stopping power) to 63% (P450). One wiki-record chain narrowed a shared ancilla register 288 -> 231 -> 210 qubits. A dead-end note proving a shortcut fails stopped two other teams' proposals; helper Lean modules were reused across teams. Paper: 'Machine-checked verification is also what makes open collaboration safe at this scale, letting teams build on one another's Lean proofs without manual code review.' Resources still exceed first error-corrected machines' likely budgets.

candidates.title: What 5,400 Malicious npm Packages Reveal about Software Supply Chain Risk in 2026
candidates.author: Databricks Threat Research: Alessandra Rizzo, Panos Sakkos, Ariel Ropek
candidates.event_date: dataset Dec 2025 - Oct 2026; registry status checked 2026-11-06
candidates.what_changed: First-year analysis after npm revoked classic long-lived tokens (Dec 9, 2025): ~5,400 confirmed malicious npm packages, including a distinct class targeting AI dev tooling (malicious MCP servers, packages that modify AI assistant config/instruction files, AI-key stealers).
candidates.mechanism: Scanner on npm publish events; kept only packages with at least one independent source (advisory, vendor campaign report, npm takedown, analyst review). Unit = package version, dated by first malicious version; monthly download snapshots.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor telemetry with precision filter; methodology described; good-quality descriptive stats, no external replication.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Partial: 87% of packages have public OSV advisories; specific campaign numbers not independently confirmed.
candidates.relevance: High: concrete controls for teams running coding agents and MCP hosts; 'protect AI assistant configuration as a credential store'.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: E3 security story ('plumbing around your models is the attack surface') is adjacent; this is new data.
candidates.summary: Compromised legit packages = 7% of set but >99% of downloads; attacker-created = 89% of set, 0.2% of downloads; 81% of attacker-created had zero downloads; top 10 packages = >99% of downloads, all compromised legit. 54% declare a lifecycle script (rest run on import/invocation); biggest campaign (>1,000 packages aimed at one org) used lifecycle scripts in 1%. Of trusted-published (OIDC) packages, 85% are compromises; August 2026 worm's highest-exposure victims republished via trusted publishing from compromised CI. 38% talk to legitimate services (serverless incl. several hundred on Cloudflare Workers, paste/code hosts, Telegram/Discord/Slack webhooks, blockchain RPC dead-drops). AI-dev credential targeting steady at 1-4% of packages; 80% of AI-key stealers target nothing else; half of MCP-abuse packages read cloud credentials. npm-token theft peaked 22% (Mar 2026), <5% from May. 78% of compromised versions add/modify a lifecycle script; 23% change maintainer/publisher. 72% obfuscated; 30% fetch second stage. 99% single-maintainer accounts; 55% free-mail; 88% <30 days old; 75% no repo; 65% retain npm init template values; 17% internal-looking names; typosquatting a minority (13% embed popular name, <5% within two edits). >300 org scopes squatted. Advisory median 1.7 days for unattributed (DPRK 4.5 days); npm takedown median 7.1 days, 10% >59 days; 37% self-unpublished by attacker at median 0.3 days (7 hours); 16% still installable. Recommendations: install-script blocking only partial -> add lockfile integrity + registry proxy with allowlist/minimum-age; diff lifecycle scripts between versions; short-lived job-scoped CI credentials; treat trusted publishing as provenance not assurance (pin CI actions, no secrets in PR builds); allowlist-based build egress; register org scopes, resolve internal scopes only internally; file-integrity monitoring on assistant config dirs, MCP host config, instruction files (like SSH keys); prepare for agent-operated intrusions (canary credentials, guardrail-tripping content, SOC detections for API-call bursts and credential use seconds after discovery).

candidates.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
candidates.author: OpenAI (customer story; quotes Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood)
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-24 (page shows November 24, 2026; RSS pubDate Tue, 24 Nov 2026 00:00 GMT)
candidates.what_changed: iFood described its internal Remote Agents Platform: coding-agent tasks exposed as a REST API, run in isolated sandboxes, returning merge requests.
candidates.mechanism: REST call submits prompt + environment requirements; dedicated remote runner in isolated Ubuntu sandbox (Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, Go; access to Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, AWS). Deterministic steps bookend the agent: clone repo, import skills, create branch; then agentic execution (GPT-5.6 Luna); then publish MR and artifacts. Post-session result parsed with Structured Outputs against a predefined contract so every run yields a machine-readable success/failure. Modeled on OpenAI Batch API and Agents API (async submit, retrieve later).
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor-published customer story; self-reported numbers, no methodology for 'accuracy doubled'.
candidates.relevance: High, actionable architecture pattern: deterministic bookends around agent step, contract-shaped completion report, cost per run as design constraint, async delegation.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to E3 'check a record it can't edit' and E2 cost-per-task stories; new URL.
candidates.summary: 15,000+ repos; >25,000 runs; >27 billion tokens; average US$0.04 inference cost per run; all runs on GPT-5.6 Luna (chosen for intelligence/efficiency/speed balance). First big user: internal security platform scanning all repos for vulnerable dependencies; after migration, fix accuracy and number of vulnerabilities resolved 'more than doubled'. Lessons listed: bottleneck is runtime not use case; combine deterministic steps with agentic execution; treat cost per run as architectural; require outputs to follow a contract; async execution is the real gain. Tips: expose agents via internal API; isolate each run with toolchains preinstalled; start with a high-volume internal user.

candidates.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
candidates.author: OpenAI (no byline); quote from Greg Brockman
candidates.what_changed: Open-source (BSD-2; BPF programs dual BSD/GPL) Linux runtime that deploys eBPF 'shields' to block vulnerable code paths on running systems while patches roll out; designed for agents to generate and validate shields with human approval.
candidates.mechanism: eBPF programs attached at kernel/process points; operators can observe a proposed shield's effect before enforcing; shields cryptographically signed and verified before load; eBPF verifier + kernel security controls; TPM-backed verifiable record of protections loaded/removed. Agents get programmable controls to investigate vulns, develop shields and validate against exploits and real workloads; security teams control deployment.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor announcement; one controlled demo (Codex-generated shield adding an input check to Java's Base64 decoder on a running Elasticsearch process blocked a 'Java4Shell' exploit without restart). Linked Isovalent write-up, GitHub repo and docs were unreachable (proxy 403 / GitHub 403) - details beyond the OpenAI page UNVERIFIED.
candidates.independent_confirmation: none (Isovalent post is partner content, not reachable)
candidates.relevance: Medium-high for platform/security ops: agent-generated mitigations behind a monitor-then-enforce, signed, human-approved gate.
candidates.summary: Four capabilities: live protection (no restart; monitor before enforce), defense at machine speed (agents propose/validate shields; humans approve), trusted deployment (signed shields, eBPF verifier), hardware-backed verification (TPM attestation log). Goal: publish tested shields alongside vulnerability disclosures; long-term auto-generated least-privilege policies. Resources: GitHub shirudo-dev/shirudo, docs.shirudo.dev VM quickstart, Isovalent self-guided lab, Dec 15 webinar, Linux Plumbers Conference walkthrough. 'Java4Shell' vulnerability name as given on page (UNVERIFIED independently).

candidates.title: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (beta) and Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API with EFS/EDC
candidates.author: Anthropic (release notes/docs); AWS ML Blog (no byline captured)
candidates.pub_date: AWS: 2026-11-23T21:01:14-08:00 (= 2026-11-24 05:01 UTC); Anthropic release notes entry dated November 23, 2026
candidates.what_changed: Anthropic launched EFS in beta on Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS and Claude on Google Cloud: ZDR for its most capable models where encrypted 'Sealed Safety Data' goes to a bucket in the customer's own cloud account and the customer's team (not Anthropic) reviews Safety Cases. AWS made its trusted access program API GA, with EFS and EDC in public preview on Bedrock. Same-day Anthropic notes: Opus 4.5 deprecated (API retirement Jan 22, 2027; migrate to Opus 5.5); org webhooks gain external_storage.failed / external_storage.recovered events; Enterprise Analytics API undercount fixes.
candidates.mechanism: Bedrock: writes prompt+response encrypted with customer KMS key to customer S3 within minutes (retries up to 72h); automated safety monitoring in AWS accounts scans across requests; Cases land under review-cases/, transcripts under transcripts/, customer writes verdicts (violation/no_violation + policy category) to review-responses/. Bedrock stops serving covered models 24h after losing access to key/bucket. EDC = same monitoring, Amazon-managed storage/keys, up to 30 days. Config per Region. Enrollment via 'aws bedrock list-trusted-access-programs' (eligible/requestable), gated by IAM/SCPs. Joining preview disables interim ZDR exception. Claude Platform: EFS applies to an entire workspace (all models); customers can't read Sealed Safety Data even in their own bucket; EFS does not cover data stored by platform features (code execution containers, Files API, Batch results, Managed Agents sessions).
candidates.evidence_quality: Primary vendor docs and release notes.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Two vendors' primary docs agree on core design.
candidates.relevance: High for platform/compliance teams using frontier Claude models: new data-handling option, alerting via webhooks, migration deadline for Opus 4.5.
candidates.summary: Bedrock routes for Claude Fable: standard aws_review retention up to 30 days; interim ZDR exception for current Fable + CVP models for internal use through at least June 30, 2027; EFS (your S3, your KMS, Bedrock keeps no copy, lifecycle minimum 30 days, CloudTrail shows Bedrock's key/bucket use); EDC (Amazon-managed, up to 30 days, cases not delivered during preview). AWS says EFS was designed with over 100 customers incl. a quarter of the Fortune 100. Covered on Bedrock: Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Opus 5.5/Sonnet 5.5 via Cyber Verification Program. Monitoring targets cross-request patterns (e.g., offensive cyber ops; agents overreaching such as exploiting software to reach an internal system). Anthropic: no charge for EFS; no change to behavior, pricing or rate limits. Supporting URLs: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview , https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/enterprise-frontier-safeguards/overview

candidates.title: The Agent Lake
candidates.author: Sam Crowder
candidates.what_changed: LangChain frames LangSmith as an 'agent lake': trace-optimized storage (SmithDB) plus 'intelligent compute' (online evaluators, decision-model-based AI Search, Insights, LangSmith Engine, SmithTune) over traces and outcomes.
candidates.mechanism: Traces + outcomes stored together; outcomes may map 1:1 (thumbs-down on a trace) or many:many (merged PRs vs threads in coding-agent type); sources = user feedback, system observation (merged PRs, copied snippets), LLM-as-judge, annotation queues. Cheap 'decision models' used as semantic filters over search results and as low-cost online evaluators. Engine clusters recurring failures into issues, diagnoses root cause, proposes PR, and (v2) tests fix against eval set. SmithTune fine-tunes on best trajectories via Fireworks/Baseten.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor marketing with a few internal numbers; IssueBench is internal.
candidates.relevance: Medium: useful framing (store outcomes next to traces; cheap classifiers for online evals) but product-centric.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: E4 used LangChain knowledge-factory post; E2 had LangSmith-adjacent items; new URL.
candidates.summary: LangSmith ingests traces from billions of agent runs/month; Clay sends hundreds of millions of events/day. Engine has analyzed >60 million production traces. SmithTune on Engine: fine-tuned Kimi K3 scored 96 on an IssueBench subset vs 90 base Kimi K3 and 87 GPT-5.6 Sol. Decision models from TypeSafe AI (introduced September) used for affordable trace classification.

candidates.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
candidates.author: Avijit Ghosh, Ben Burtenshaw, Irene Solaiman
candidates.what_changed: Eight-step guide (claim, find task, run unchanged, adapt, check eval, read traces, report score, compare models) using Harbor + Terminal-Bench raman-fitting adapted into 'raman-lab', plus a component-by-component table of what to open vs protect.
candidates.mechanism: Before model runs, test the evaluation: reference solution must pass; do-nothing agent and a deliberate shortcut must fail. Their shortcut (read peak heights, guess widths) got the defect ratio right on all 8 tasks, so they added per-peak fit checks. Read traces to separate failure types; report pass@k and pass^k; pin inference provider for open-weight models.
candidates.evidence_quality: Small worked example (8 dev tasks, 3 rollouts) with explicit caveats; cites external audits.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Cited audits (Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified audit, CritPt) are third-party/primary claims not re-checked here.
candidates.relevance: High for eval builders, but heavily overlaps E4's 'audit the grader' story.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Substantial overlap with E4 Evaluation story (grader audits; HF harness-adapters post). New material: worked shortcut-test procedure and open/protect table.
candidates.summary: Harness change with fixed model moved Terminal-Bench accuracy by up to 29.9 pp. 98.2% of model-benchmark scores reported by one party only. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5: 60% private/held-out. Baseline gpt-oss-120b 0/3 on original task (two early completion declarations, one decimal-comma parse failure). raman-lab: 11/24 rollouts passed; in 19 the model called mark_task_complete in its first response, 11 of those with no results file; only 2 of 13 failures failed the fit check; pass@3 7/8, pass^3 1/8; mean 0.46, SE ~0.11 clustered by task; repeat run 10/24; with DeepInfra pinned 13/24. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 (tasks can't rank them). Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of 89 tasks after user reports; CritPt audit found errors in 21 of 56; OpenAI SWE-bench Verified audit: issues in 59.4% of 138 problems; OpenAI estimated ~30% of SWE-Bench Pro broken (July 2026). Hub: ~3,500 eval leaderboards, ~17,000 eval datasets (16x in a year).

candidates.title: Working with AI
candidates.author: Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
candidates.what_changed: 66 interviews at 58 US enterprise customers on how AI adoption reorganizes work; finds value comes mostly from reorganization, few layoffs but reduced hiring.
candidates.mechanism: Interviews coded by an automated coder (value, org change 0-100, bottlenecks, task reallocations); non-random sample of Anthropic customers; self-reported value.
candidates.evidence_quality: Qualitative, non-representative, vendor's own customers; self-reported value.
candidates.relevance: Medium: org-level practitioner lessons (code review as bottleneck, maintenance cost of vibe-coded apps, shared data infrastructure, 'skill.md' editing roles).
candidates.summary: ~300 AI applications coded; 100 pieces of AI-written software described in detail: 80% automated manual work, 20% replaced existing (often vendor) software; Figure 3 covers 140 pieces by role/purpose. Layoffs rare: 5 companies pushed out non-adopters, 2 saw automation eliminate a position; 10 hired more; two-thirds reported reduced hiring; 9 cut contractors (often offshore), one finance company >100 offshore contractors. Approval-workflow agent cut planned reviewer hiring >90% but reviewers resisted (some 2 min/submission, some 10+). Six startups estimated needing on average 4x headcount without AI; one COO: 90% of ops budget on tokens. Bottlenecks: review of AI output, uneven acceleration (an agent's errant 'S' on an API endpoint broke a release), uneven adoption, missing context/infra; customer skepticism and regulation rarely cited. Engineer who automated production-alert tickets read every transcript for two months and still samples every two weeks at six months. Recommendations: broaden roles, redeploy to bottleneck tasks, build shared infra and agent-accessible data.

candidates.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

candidates.mechanism: Model writes and runs code to design 3D structures; specialized models (SolubleMPNN, ProteinMPNN, ESMFold) used for sequences/selection in some experiments.
candidates.evidence_quality: Preprint + wet-lab results with partner; hit rates lower than RFdiffusion original study (OpenAI notes filtering differences).
candidates.relevance: Low for practitioner lens (science); possible research-corner item.
candidates.summary: Minibinders: 322 tested vs 5 targets, 35 (10.9%) bound (PD-L1 5, IL-7Ra 3, TrkA 1, VEGF-A 8, IL-17A 18). VHH loop redesign vs IL-4Ra 128/182 (70%); therapeutic antibody fragments 179/272 (66%). Motif scaffolding (30 MotifBench): internal model 43.7% vs RFdiffusion 27.8%; fold design (200 CATH): 18.9% vs Proteina 17.1%. Full structure prediction a clear weakness. 14 protein tasks evaluated.
